text: {"boxes":[{"excerpt":"The IMF’s data on the currency composition of foreign exchange (FX) reserves is scrutinized carefully for any signs that the world is shifting way from the dollar.","claim":"Is the dollar's global role really measured by its share in central bank FX reserves, or is the action elsewhere?","role":"question","explicit":false,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[2,3,5],"reason":"Ask whether the most-watched statistic actually captures where a phenomenon is changing."},{"excerpt":"Yet it doesn’t really matter that much if the dollar’s share of reserves has shifted from 56.5 percent to 57 percent. The ink-to-impact ratio of the quarterly reporting on the latest COFER data is all off.","claim":"Analysts who pore over quarterly COFER shares for signs of de-dollarization are focused on the wrong data.","role":"opposing_view","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[2,3,41],"reason":"Small shifts in a static stock matter less than where new flows are going."},{"excerpt":"Neither the stock of global reserves nor the stock of dollar reserves has changed much in the last ten years.","claim":"Global reserves and dollar reserves have been roughly flat for a decade, including Japan's and Korea's.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[4,25,30],"reason":"A stock that has stopped growing cannot be the source of new inflows."},{"excerpt":"","claim":"Assets held by pension funds, state banks, sovereign funds and state-steered insurers are effectively public-sector foreign assets comparable to reserves.","role":"hidden_assumption","explicit":false,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[7,9,13,32,33],"reason":"Ownership or control by the state, not the legal label of the holder, determines whether assets are official."},{"excerpt":"China’s state banks (per the Bank of International Settlements) have almost as many foreign assets as the central bank (PBOC).","claim":"Quasi-sovereign pools now rival formal reserves in China, Japan, Korea and Saudi Arabia, and Taiwan's lifers play a similar policy role.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[6,7,8,9,11,36],"reason":"Compare the size of alternative state pools with the official measure to judge its coverage."},{"excerpt":"Asia’s big surplus economies are in a sense just catching up with the world’s oil exporters. Norway put its oil surplus into a sovereign wealth fund from the start.","claim":"Asian surplus economies are following oil exporters in routing surpluses into sovereign funds rather than central bank reserves.","role":"mechanism","explicit":true,"kind":"economic","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[11],"reason":"Governments with persistent surpluses shift savings toward return-seeking vehicles over time."},{"excerpt":"So too does the PBOC’s use of the “macroprudential adjustment factor” effectively adjust banks’ net foreign assets in much the same way that CBC regulations adjust lifer hedge ratios.","claim":"Central banks steer currency by regulating hedge ratios and bank net foreign assets, moving foreign asset accumulation off their own books.","role":"mechanism","explicit":true,"kind":"economic","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[9,10,33],"reason":"Regulating private balance sheets can substitute for direct intervention."},{"excerpt":"China reports $3.3 trillion in gross foreign assets to the BIS","claim":"China's state banks hold $3.3 trillion gross foreign assets (BIS), ~$4 trillion BOP outflows, $2.5 trillion at top five banks, and policy banks nearly $1 trillion; net bank outflows exceeded reserve accumulation since 2010.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[15,16,17,18],"reason":"Cross-check balance-of-payments flows against banking and balance sheet stocks."},{"excerpt":"But the work of AidData points to nearly $1 trillion in foreign assets, with a hefty dollar share.","claim":"BIS data, SAFE disclosures, bank annual reports and AidData research all point to large, dollar-heavy state bank assets.","role":"evidence_source","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[16,18,19,21],"reason":"Independent sources agreeing strengthen an estimate of undisclosed holdings."},{"excerpt":"with at this stage the complicity of the IMF, which has neither analyzed the role of SAFE policy bank financing, nor highlighted the glaring gap in China’s own reporting","claim":"China does not disclose policy bank foreign assets and the IMF has failed to flag the gap, so official reporting is incomplete.","role":"source_credibility","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[19],"reason":"Treat gaps tolerated by the official data steward as a reason to look beyond its datasets."},{"excerpt":"SAFE’s disclosure—which covers the commercial banks—puts the dollar share of their offshore foreign currency assets at around 70 percent. That is well above the last disclosed dollar share of China’s formal reserves (55 percent in 2019).","claim":"Dollar shares of quasi-sovereign pools are high: ~70% for Chinese banks, ~70% for NPS, over 95% for Taiwan lifers, ~80% for PIF, versus 55% in China's reserves.","role":"evidence_data","explicit":true,"kind":"none","claim_type":"none","paragraphs":[12,21,27,28,31,33,35],"reason":"Compare currency composition across holders to see where dollar demand
